paras: The hunt for a Black suspect in the Seward murder was a manhunt in Putnam County, Indiana, after Mrs. Henry Seward was beaten to death in her farmhouse near Fern station, west of Greencastle, on May 16, 1903. Searching parties hunted a Black tramp seen boarding a freight train near the house, and a widely reprinted dispatch said they threatened to lynch him if caught. No Black suspect was reported caught, and within days suspicion turned to the woman's husband, who was jailed in July and held for the murder.
Henry Seward and his wife had been married less than a year and had just begun housekeeping on their own farm, a mile and a half west of Fern station, close to the Big Four Railroad.

Seward said he found his wife's body when he came home from farm work at about 6 o'clock, her head crushed by blows from a club. Suspicion fell at once on "a negro tramp" who had been seen climbing onto a westbound freight train about 4:45 that afternoon.

On May 17, according to a Terre Haute dispatch, a bloody club about four feet long was found some 200 yards from the house, and descriptions of the suspect were sent through the surrounding country. In the Louisville Courier-Journal's copy, the dispatch added that "threats are made by searching parties that he will be lynched if caught." The Indianapolis Journal's Greencastle correspondent described the excitement near the farm as intense and wrote that if any Black man had been found on a freight train and taken back to Fern, "his life undoubtedly would have been a thing of small value." No report that a Black man was caught or harmed appears in the coverage.

By May 18 the Journal reported that "public sentiment has thoroughly shifted" toward the husband, noting that the tramp theory had been "suggested by Seward" and that his arrest seemed likely. Seward denied any quarrel, while his father argued that the tramp had climbed in a window to steal and killed Mrs. Seward to keep her from raising an alarm. The coroner's investigation on May 20 found no strong evidence against anyone, and the Plymouth Tribune reported that the husband had cleared himself.

By mid-July, however, Henry Seward was in jail for his wife's murder, and the Journal reported claims that the killing copied one in a detective story found in his home. At his preliminary hearing in late July, one witness said Seward had threatened to "bump" his wife, and another that he once said "Just because I killed my wife" before correcting himself. A Journal headline the next day reported that Seward was held for the murder; no report of a trial was found.

Readers outside Indiana learned of the case through the Terre Haute dispatch of May 17, which placed the murder near Lena and named the victim "Mrs. Hauck Stewart." Headlines named the suspect by race: the Omaha Daily Bee's "Citizens Search for Negro" and the Bemidji Daily Pioneer's "Searching Parties Looking for Negro Suspected of Murder." The Bee's subhead treated the man as guilty, "Hold Black Person Guildy [Guilty] of Brutal Murder," although its text, unlike the Courier-Journal's and the Pioneer's, left out the lynching threat.

A second dispatch told a different story: printed in the Indianapolis Journal on May 17 and the New York Sun on May 18, it said "three foreigners" were believed to have committed the assault and made no mention of a Black suspect. That version ran as late as June 3 in the Abbeville Press and Banner of South Carolina. The Indianapolis Journal, through its own Greencastle correspondent, followed the case most closely, reporting the shift of suspicion from the tramp to the husband and then his arrest and hearing. No Black newspaper account of the episode was found.

Accounts of the suspect differed from the start: the Terre Haute wire and the Journal's correspondent named a Black tramp, while the earlier dispatch blamed "three foreigners." The dispatches also gave the victim's name as "Hauck," "Huack" or "Quack" Stewart; the local Greencastle reports call her Mrs. Henry Seward.

bases: Searching parties hunting an unnamed Black tramp suspected of a murder were reported to threaten to lynch him if caught (A2, A5); no Black person was reported caught or harmed, so this is a threatened lynching in a manhunt (A5, A11).

No one was killed: the Black suspect was never reported caught (A5, A11), and suspicion moved to the victim's husband, who was jailed and given a hearing (A24, A27). The threat to lynch was made under the pretext of punishing a murder (A2).

The Terre Haute wire (A2, A3) and the Indianapolis Journal's own Greencastle correspondent (A5, A11) independently report that a Black tramp was suspected and hunted and that he would have been in danger if caught, though a separate dispatch blamed 'three foreigners' (A1, A4).

accounts.label: Terre Haute wire (May 17)
accounts.gist: Searching parties scouring the country around Lena for the Black man put off a train near the house, who was thought to be the murderer; descriptions sent out and, in some copies, threats that he would be lynched if caught.

accounts.label: 'Three foreigners' dispatch
accounts.gist: Mrs. 'Huack' or 'Quack' Stewart was assaulted and murdered while her husband plowed nearby; three foreigners were believed guilty and posses were searching for them.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal Greencastle correspondent
accounts.gist: A Black tramp was first presumed guilty and would have been in danger if caught; within two days suspicion shifted to the husband, who had suggested the tramp theory.

accounts.label: Seward family
accounts.gist: Henry Seward denied any quarrel; his father argued the tramp entered by a window and killed Mrs. Seward to avoid an alarm.

framing.detail: Out-of-state papers ran the Terre Haute wire under headlines naming a 'Negro' as the suspect ('Citizens Search for Negro'; 'Searching Parties Looking for Negro Suspected of Murder'); the Courier-Journal and Bemidji copies repeated the lynching threat without comment.
The Omaha Daily Bee's subhead treated the suspect as guilty ('Hold Black Person Guildy of Brutal Murder') though its text said only that he was 'thought' responsible.
The Indianapolis Journal's correspondent noted matter-of-factly that a Black man brought back to Fern would have been in danger, then followed the case as suspicion turned to the husband.

The Greencastle correspondent's reports and the later coverage use Seward; 'Hauck Stewart' looks like a garble of 'Henry Seward'.
